style: Matte astronomy paintings and exact phase/geometry diagrams
provider: Built-in image generation and deterministic SVG diagrams
note: Images are text-free with editable captions. Distinguish Earth-view phase disks from space-view position diagrams: orbit pictures show the Sun-facing hemisphere, not the phase seen from Earth. Right-lit waxing examples use a northern-up textbook convention; viewing orientation varies with location and time. Dark outlines make the new Moon’s position visible in diagrams, not in the real night sky. All sizes, distances, shadow cones and orbital planes are simplified and not to scale. Lunar surface textures are artistic. Ordinary phases are not caused by Earth’s shadow. Keep the model ball out of the observer’s head shadow for a full phase; deliberately align it only when demonstrating an eclipse. Use a cool lamp and blunt handle with teacher supervision, never direct solar viewing or a laser. Educator review remains pending.

sources.prompt: Square astronomy teaching illustration in matte gouache and gentle screen-print grain, deep navy background, restrained cream and cool gray, not photographic or glossy 3D. A single large circular Moon centered with generous margins. No stars, planets, people, labels, text, letters, numbers, arrows, logos or watermark. Surface marks are subtle and illustrative, not a claim to be a geographically exact lunar map. Clearly distinguish the illuminated surface from the dark portion. Show a waxing crescent in a northern-up textbook orientation: a very thin cream crescent follows the RIGHT circular rim, tapering to tips at top and bottom. Only about fifteen percent of the disk is bright; the rest is very dark navy. The outer limb stays a circle; the inner boundary curves to the right too.
sources.alt: A thin pale crescent follows the right rim of a dark circular Moon against navy.

assets.caption: Space view: sunlight comes from the left. Earth is central. The Moon at left is at new moon, below is first quarter, right is full, and above is third quarter in this north-of-orbit view. Every drawn Moon is half illuminated toward the Sun. These are positions, not the phase shapes seen from Earth. Sizes, distances and tilt are simplified.
assets.prompt: Exact text-free diagram: A Sun at left sends arrows rightward toward Earth and four Moon positions; every small Moon has its left half illuminated.

assets.caption: Read the top row left to right, then the bottom row left to right: new, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full, waning gibbous, third quarter, waning crescent. The cycle averages 29.5 days. Orientation is a northern-up textbook convention; sky orientation varies.

assets.caption: Lunar eclipse geometry: Sun–Earth–Moon. The Moon is near full and enters Earth’s shadow. Total lunar eclipses can look copper red; partial and penumbral eclipses look different. Only the central shadow is shown. Sizes and distances are not to scale.

assets.caption: This is Earth’s central shadow in a lunar-eclipse alignment. Ordinary Moon phases are not caused by this shadow. The outer partial-shadow region is omitted; the picture is not to scale.

assets.caption: Each disk is the Moon at a different time. The golden marker identifies the same surface region, not the lit side. Keeping it toward Earth requires one rotation per orbit, about 27.3 days relative to the stars. Libration lets us see a little around the edges over time.
